content: A body temperature of 41°C (106°F) or higher is classified as hyperpyrexia, which is an extremely high fever. This condition is distinct from hyperthermia. In hyperpyrexia, the body’s temperature regulation mechanism actively sets the body temperature to an abnormally high level. In contrast, hyperthermia occurs when the body’s temperature exceeds the set point due to external factors or an inability to dissipate heat. Differential Diagnosis of Hyperpyrexia Causes: 1. Excessive Heat or Sun Exposure: Prolonged exposure to high environmental temperatures or direct sunlight can lead to heat hyperpyrexia, a component of heatstroke. 2. Stimulant Abuse: The use of amphetamines or other stimulants can exacerbate the effects of heat hyperpyrexia, increasing the risk of dangerously high body temperatures. 3. Withdrawal from Depressants: Withdrawal from substances such as barbiturates, alcohol, or other anxiolytics can occasionally result in hyperpyrexia. This is less commonly observed with benzodiazepine withdrawal. 4. Septicemia: A systemic bacterial infection of the bloodstream can lead to hyperpyrexia as part of the body’s inflammatory response. 5. Viral Infections: Certain viral infections, such as infectious mononucleosis, can also cause hyperpyrexia. 6. Thyrotoxic Crisis: In cases of hyperthyroidism, a thyrotoxic crisis can result in dangerously elevated body temperatures. 7. Malignant Hyperpyrexia: This condition arises from the breakdown of muscle tissue following over-excitation, triggered by specific stimuli. These triggers may include extreme physical exertion (especially in high ambient temperatures), prolonged and intense convulsions, certain anesthetic agents, fever, or drugs such as cocaine, alcohol, and aspirin. 8. Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS): This syndrome can occur following the administration of antipsychotic medications and is characterized by hyperpyrexia among other symptoms.
